PUBLIC COMMENT RULES

“(California Government Code Section 54954.3).
(a) Every agenda for a special meeting shall provide an opportunity for members of the
public to directly address the legislative body on any item that has been described in the
notice for the meeting, before or during the legislative body’s consideration of the item,
that is within the subject matter jurisdiction of the legislative body, provided that no action
shall be taken on any item not appearing on the agenda unless the action is otherwise
authorized by subdivision (b) of Section 54954.2 [section omitted].

(b) (1) The legislative body of a local agency may adopt reasonable regulations to ensure
that the intent of the subdivision (a) is carried out, including, but not limited to, regulations
limiting the total amount of time allocated for public testimony on particular issues and for
each individual speaker.
  (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), when the legislative body of a local agency limits
time for public comment, the legislative body of a local agency shall provide at least twice
the allotted time to a member of the public who utilizes a translator to ensure that non-
English speakers receive the same opportunity to directly address the legislative body of

Planning Commission  Thursday, January 16, 2025
 a local agency.”

In furtherance of Section 54954.3 of the Brown Act, the public is allotted to speak a total
of two (2) minutes on the entirety of the Consent Calendar, Appointment(s), with two (2)
minutes on each Public Hearing, and, if desired, an additional two (2) minutes on items
not on the agenda that are within the subject matter jurisdiction of the Planning
Commission. As specified in the Brown Act, a speaker utilizing a translator will receive
twice the amount of time specified.

  6.A  Adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-026, a Resolution of the Planning Commission
  of the City of Palmdale, approving Variance 24-0002; a request to allow the
  installation of an on-site wastewater treatment facility to facilitate the future
  construction of a single-family residence located at the northeast corner of
  Pearblossom Highway and 60th Street East and finding that the project is
  categorically exempt from environmental review.

  Staff presentation by Planning Manager Magaña. The proposed application would
  allow the installation of an on-site wastewater treatment facility to facilitate the
  construction of a single-family residence on a vacant 0.73-acre lot located on the
  northeast corner of Pearblossom Highway and 60th Street East. Staff and the applicant
  is available for questions.

  Chair Henderson opened the public hearing.

  No comments received.

  Chair Henderson closed the public hearing.

  Motion: Adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-026
  Moved by: Commissioner Olivarez and seconded by Commissioner Lujan
  Vote: Motion carried 4 - 1
  Abstain: 0
  Absent: 1

  6.B  Adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-024; a Resolution of the Planning Commission of
  the City of Palmdale recommending City Council approval of Time Extension 24-
  0006 and Major Modification 24-0008 and finding that the proposed project is
  consistent with the previously adopted Mitigated Negative Declaration.

  Staff presentation by Planning Manager Magaña and noted the TTM 60500 was
  originally approved by the Planning Commission on September 21, 2006. The
  applicant requests approval for a two-year extension and a Major Modification to
  phase the TTM into four separate phases. The applicant has used all discretionary
  extensions available through the Palmdale Municipal Code and the Subdivision Map
  Act.

  Public testimony was received in opposition to the project and expressed the following
  concerns related to public notification, traffic impact study, fire hazard area, mountain
  lions, Joshua tree conservation impacts.
 Traffic Manager Jay Nelson addressed the traffic concerns related to speed. This
project will not have a significant impact on traffic on Rancho Vista Blvd.

Planning Manager Magaña addressed the public notification sent via US Postal mail
as well as a public hearing notice sign located on the project site. The California
Department of Fish and Wildlife will require an incidental take permits for the removal
of Joshua Trees.

Commissioner Jones inquired about the fire safety concerns and wildlife.

Planning Manager Magana noted that once the builder is identified, the property will
have to meet the fire codes. The project is conditioned to give nesting bird surveys and
surveys on the land prior to building.

Chair Henderson opened the public hearing.

No comments received.

Chair Henderson closed the public hearing.

Motion: Adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-024
Moved by: Commissioner Olivarez and seconded by Commissioner Jones
Vote: Motion carried 4-1
Abstain: 0
Absent: 1

6.C  Adopt Resolution PC-2024-027, a Resolution of the Planning Commission of the
  City of Palmdale, recommending City Council approval of Specific Plan 22-001,

  Agreement 22-001, Environmental Impact Report 22-001, Tentative Parcel Map
  83738, and Site Plan Review 22-008 to subdivide the 432.9-acre site into 19
  parcels for the phased development of a master-planned commerce center
  containing industrial, commercial, and open space, with all required on-site and
  off-site improvements and infrastructure. The phases of development would
  allow for a maximum of 8,302,536 square feet of building footprint, to be
  comprised of approximately 8,241,552 square feet of industrial and 60,984
  square feet of commercial uses

Staff presentation, Planning Manager Magaña noted that the project buildout is
proposed in four phases. The required entitlements for the project have been outlined
   in the conditions of approval. Both the applicant and staff are available to answer any
  questions.

  Chair Henderson opened the public hearing.

  Public testimony was received by union representatives from the following; the
  Coalition for Racial & Ethnic Equity in Development (CREED), Laborers’ Union of
  North America (LUNA), United Auto Workers, Local 1761, and Western States
  Regional Council of Carpenters (WSRCC) on this item in support of this project.

  Chair Henderson closed the public hearing.

  Chair Henderson asked if Air Force Plant 42 had any concerns about the flyover space
  as it relates to the project.

  Planning Manager Magaña stated that Air Force Plant 42 was notified at the project’s
  initial stage, and no comments were received.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommends that the Planning Commission adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-029, a
Resolution of the Planning Commission of the City of Palmdale recommending City
Council approval of Comprehensive Development (CDEV) 23-0002, Conditional Use
Permit (CUP) 23-0018, and Vesting Tentative Tract Maps 23-0003 (VTTM 51508-3) and
23-0004 (VTTM 63145) to facilitate the development of approximately 75 acres for the
purpose of constructing 627 single-family residences within Phase 1B of the Ritter Ranch
Specific Plan and find that the project includes minor alterations to the previously adopted
Environmental Impact Report (EIR 90-4) prepared for the previously approved project as
outlined within the addendum.

BACKGROUND

On February 27, 1992, EIR 90-4 (SCH No. 90010124) was certified by the City of
Palmdale for the development of a 10,625-acre master-planned community consisting of
7,200 residences, 7,600 acres of open space and the necessary public facilities,
recreational amenities, schools, and commercial uses to support the community.
 Staff Report to Planning Commission
CD 23-0002, CUP23-0018, & VTTM’s 23-0003/23-0004
January 16, 2025
Page 2

On March 3, 1992, the City adopted Ordinance No. 964, approving the Ritter Ranch
Specific Plan (SP). The approvals included: General Plan Amendment 91-3, Pre-zone
89-12, SP 89-02, and Development Agreement (DA) 92-1. As originally approved, the SP
was intended to encompass all actions associated with the implementation and
development of the properties within the SP Area. The SP manages the use of land,
establishes provisions for site development, and provides a comprehensive approach to
infrastructure planning and financing.

In 1995, DA 92-1 was amended to define the responsibility of the City and the applicant
to fund and construct various infrastructure improvements and provided the applicant with
assurance that the development standards within the SP would remain in place without
change.

On October 11, 1995, the City approved Specific Plan Amendment 95-1-RR (Ordinance
No. 1076), which amended the SP to reflect the provisions of the Agreement of
Compromise, Settlement and Release between Ritter Park Associates, the Leona Valley
Town Council and the City of Palmdale and amended and corrected certain portions of
the SP. The changes included the phasing of various infrastructure and amenities,
reductions in the number of dwelling units in portions of the project, restrictions on
allowable commercial uses in some portions of the project, and various minor text
changes.

In December 1995, the City approved six VTTMs (51604, 51605, 51606, 51607, 52093
and 52116), collectively known as Phase 1A, and although the maps were not recorded,
the lots were graded and internal roadways were partially installed (i.e. final paving was
not completed). After a series of automatic and discretionary extensions of time, all six
VTTM's expired on January 20, 2017.

A revised DA for the SP was approved in 2004 (2004 DA), replacing the original DA 92-
1. Similar to DA 92-1, 2004 DA defined the responsibility of the City and the applicant to
fund and construct various infrastructure improvements and provided the applicant with
assurance that the development standards specified within the SP would remain in
applicable to the project. In June 2012, the 2004 DA also subsequently expired by its own
terms.

On March 2, 2006, the City approved VTTM's 51508-03 (Resolution No. PC-2006-018)
and 63145 (Resolution No. PC-2006-019), respectively. VTTM 51508-03 was
subsequently recorded and subdivided 92.32 acres into six lots. VTTM 63145 (Lot 2 of
VTTM 51508-03), included the subdivision of 50.56 acres into 241 single-family
residential lots, three open space lots and two park lots. On August 11, 2016, the City
approved requested time extensions for both VTTM 51508-3 and 63145 (Resolution Nos.
PC-2016-031 and PC-2016-030, respectively) which subsequently expired on August 23,
2019.
 Staff Report to Planning Commission
CD 23-0002, CUP23-0018, & VTTM’s 23-0003/23-0004
January 16, 2025
Page 3

Subsequent to the VTTM expiration, mass grading consistent with VTTM 51808 was
completed, and backbone roads (Westland Drive and Ranch Center Drive) were installed.
These roadways are currently open to public travel. Portions of the required perimeter
walls along these roadways were also installed.

On February 10, 2022, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution Nos. PC-2022-005
through PC-2022-011 approving VTTM’s 51604, 51605, 51606, 51607, 52093 and
52116, CUP 22-001 and Planned Development (PD) 21-001 to facilitate the development
of 553 single-family residences on approximately 115 acres, including open space,
neighborhood and community parks, and interconnectivity within Phase 1A (Planning
Area 5) of the SP.

The current application submittal from the applicant (Phase 1B) proposes to continue the
on-going development allowed in Planning Area 5 (PA5) of the SP and is physically
adjacent to and connects to the residential project recently approved by the City for Phase
1A. Even with the construction proposed by both Phase 1A and 1B, a balance of 1,411
total dwelling of additional capacity units will remain available for potential development
in PA5 of the SP and as analyzed by EIR 90-4.

The applicant is requesting approval of a Planned Development (CDEV 23-0002) for
Phase 1B of Planning Area 5, which is implemented through a Conditional Use Permit
(CUP 23-0018) as required by the SP. In conjunction with CDEV 23-002, the applicant is
requesting approval of VTTM’s 23-0003/23-0004 to reinstate the prior approved VTTMs
51508-3 and 63145. The requested approvals would allow the subdivision of 75 acres for
the comprehensive development and construction of 627 single-family residences (135
detached and 492 attached) and the associated open space, trails, neighborhood
recreation areas, community parks, landscaping, public utility infrastructure, development
identification signs, and public roadways/bikeways.

a portion of Planning Area 5 for Single Family Attached (SFA) land use and allows other
uses through the approval of a planned development document. VTTM 63145 will
implement the portion of the site that is proposed to create the 135 single-family detached,

0002 for single-family attached, detached condo, and small lot products (492 additional

Vesting Tentative Maps

State Subdivision Laws allow property to be subdivided into 5 or more lots through
submittal of a Tentative Tract Map or Vesting Tentative Tract Map application prepared
by a State Licensed Civil Engineer or Land Surveyor to a local City or County for approval.

The City of Palmdale Municipal Code (Section 16.50.020) requires that the Planning
Commission consider all tentative maps which would create small lot subdivisions and
make a recommendation to the City Council with respect to the application’s compliance
with the General Plan, any applicable specific plan, and the zoning ordinance.

The applicant is requesting approval for two Vesting Tentative Tract Maps that previously
expired in 2019 (VTTM 51508-3 and VTTM 63145).

VTTM 23-0003 (Figure 3) is seeking to reinstate City entitlement approvals for VTTM
51508-03. This type of map is often referred to as an “A” map which is a type of
subdivision map that creates large lots but no new building sites. It is typically used to
divide land by a master developer. The map current shows 6 lots including Lot 2, which
is proposed to be subdivided by VTTM 63145.

VTTM 23-0004 (Figure 4) is seeking to reinstate City entitlement approvals for VTTM
63145, which subdivides the parcel into 135 single family detached lots.

Additional development authorized by CDEV 23-0002 on the remaining lots depicted on
VTTM 51508-03 are intended for future single family attached, detached condo, and small
lot products which will be processed through Site Plan Review and Tentative Tract Map
or Condominium Map applications in the future.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

An Environmental Impact Report (EIR) was prepared for the project in conjunction with
the original approval and on February 27, 1992, the City Council adopted EIR 90-04
(Resolution No. 92-22, SCH No. 90010124). The EIR identified potential significant
impacts with respect to: Earth Resources, Air Resources, Water Resources, Biological
Resources, Noise, Aesthetics, Land Use, Public Health and Safety, Traffic, Cultural
Resources and Public Facilities. A Statement of Overriding Consideration was adopted
by the City Council in conjunction with the original approval. In accordance with Public
Resources Code Section 21166 and State California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Guidelines Sections 15162 and 15163, the proposed project does not require the
preparation of a subsequent or supplemental to the EIR prepared for the SP (EIR 90-04)
since: 1) the project will cause no substantial changes in any portion of the project which
was described in EIR 90-4, which would require major revisions to EIR 90-4 due to the
involvement of new significant environmental effects or a substantial increase in the
severity of previously identified significant effects because the project is not modifying the
scope or intent of the SP; 2) no substantial changes have occurred with respect to the
circumstances under which the project is undertaken, which will require major revisions
to said EIR due to the involvement of new significant environmental effects or a
substantial increase in the severity of previously identified environmental effects, because
no significant development adjacent to the project area which impacts the infrastructure,
services, or development potential within the City's boundaries has occurred; and 3) no
new information of substantial importance, which was not known and could not have been
known with the exercise of reasonable diligence at the time the previous EIR was certified
as complete, has been provided with respect to the SP. As such, an addendum to the
EIR has been prepared in accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15164 and has
identified that there are no new or additional significant impacts that were not already
addressed by the EIR.

In summary, the Phase 1B project results in fewer units than what was analyzed for the
SP within EIR 90-4; the project would not have any additional or more intensive impacts
than what has already documented in the City approved Statement of Overriding
Considerations and Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program; substantial evidence
has not been documented that would warrant the preparation of a Subsequent EIR nor a
Supplemental EIR; and the preparation of an Addendum to EIR 90-4 is appropriate.

The City’s General Plan and Zoning Ordinance/Code establish the overall framework for land use and development. As allowed by
State Law, the City adopted the Ritter Ranch Specific Plan, which provides detailed land use regulations specific to the areas within
its boundaries. This Specific Plan has equivalent authority and legal standing to the City’s General Plan and Zoning regulations. Within
the planning areas of the Specific Plan, only the uses explicitly outlined are permitted, and the requirements of the Specific Plan
supersede any conflicting provisions in the General Plan or Zoning Ordinance/Code, ensuring that the Specific Plan serves as the
definitive guide for land use and development in its jurisdiction. Moreover, the Ritter Ranch Specific Plan (SP) Section 6.7.1 provides for
conditionally permitted Planned Developments (PD) within designated areas “to achieve greater flexibility in design; to encourage well-
planned neighborhoods through creative and imaginative planning” and to “promote residential amenities beyond those expected under
conventional development.” In addition, the Planned Development process provides a mechanism to approve lotting concept alternatives
within a planning area in substantial conformance with the Specific Plan.
Planned Development Application CDEV23-0002 (the PD) addresses PUs 5U, 5T (partial), 5X-1, 5X-2, 5W-4, and 5W-5. This Planned
Development provides the following:
•  Lot size standards for 5,000 square foot Single Family Detached (SFD) Lots.
•  Standards for Single Family Attached (SFA), Detached Condo, and Small Lot products.
•  Design Standards for community entry facilities, including facilities which are located outside the boundaries of this Planned
  Development.
•  Conceptual Designs for public and private parks.
Development standards not addressed in this Planned Development shall defer to the Ritter Ranch Specific Plan and the Palmdale Zoning
Code.

 4.1 ENTITLEMENT PROCESSING
The following clarifies the relationship between this PD and future entitlements:
  •  The Ritter Ranch Specific Plan (Specific Plan) provides the basic entitlement framework for the entire project. The Specific Plan
  designates the portion of PA 5 included in the PD application as Single Family Attached (SFA) land use and allows other uses
  through an approved PD.
  •  “B” Maps are tentative tract maps typically submitted for individual subdivisions required for neighborhood build out. Tentative
  Tract Map 63145 is being processed in parallel with this PD to create single family detached lots.
  •  It is anticipated the Single Family Attached, Detached Condo, and Small Lot products will be processed by Site Plan Review and
  Tentative Tract Maps or Condominium Maps.
  •  Final designs for the Neighborhood Recreation Areas, the Neighborhood Park and the Community Park are subject to review and
  approval by the City of Palmdale.

*Note: Park 5T is a proposed parcel within 51508-3 and therefore the northern portion of the park being constructed as part of Phase 1A
may be offered for dedication in advance by metes and bounds legal description.

  4.2 PHASING
 4.2.1 This PD does not establish a specific order in which each Planning Unit will be constructed. The backbone infrastructure for
 Westland Drive is existing (except water within the Phase 1B portion), and extensions of Parkview Drive and Ritter Ranch Road will
 be constructed as required to support adjacent Planning Units. Planning Units 5W-4 and 5W-5 will require the undergrounding of the
 existing channel bisecting these areas, along with construction of the proposed roadway and utilities in that alignment. Additionally,
 the construction of off-site down stream sewer improvements to service development within the Phase 1B area will be required. The
 improvements are intended to be master developer responsibilities; therefore, each individual Tentative Tract Map or Site Plan within the
 PD will be able to commence construction without waiting for infrastructure to be built out by earlier phases. This will allow the individual
 Planning Units to be developed independently of each other, in any order, when in compliance with the regulations and standards of this
 PD, as applicable.

 4.3 LANDSCAPE MAINTENANCE
 4.3.1 Within the PD boundary, landscape maintenance will be the responsibility of the following entities:
  a) Arterial right-of-way median and slope will be the responsibility of the Homeowners Association (HOA).
  b) Maintenance of temporary slopes (off-site) and temporary drainage facilities will be the responsibility of the Master Developer
  until adjacent development occurs.
  c) Maintenance of all other landscaping including landscape easements, pedestrian spines and connectors, etc. will be the
  responsibility of the HOA.
  d) Maintenance of the Neighborhood Park and the Community Parks will be the responsibility of the City of Palmdale.
  e) Maintenance of the Neighborhood Recreation Areas will be the responsibility of the HOA.
  f) The HOA is responsible for maintaining arterial medians and slopes, except in cases where a Landscape Maintenance District is
  established. For the parkways and medians along Ritter Ranch Road, maintenance will be handled by the Landscape Maintenance
  District.
  g) Maintenance of signage, identified in section 3.5, will be the responsibility of the HOA, except for signage in City maintained
  Parks.

 4.4 OPEN SPACE REQUIREMENTS
 According to the Ritter Ranch Specific Plan, a minimum of 30% of the development area must be designated as open space. Currently,
 Phase 1B is comprised of 18% parks and neighborhood recreation areas. Therefore, each residential planning unit is required to include at
 least 12% open space, contributing to the overall requirement. These requirements can be fulfilled via HOA landscaping, private yards, and
 private balconies.

ANALYSIS

The proposed project includes a GPA and ZC to modify the Land Use designation and
zone from MU 2 to NC to facilitate the development of a grocery store, fueling station,
and drive-through carwash. The project is significant for the City of Palmdale as it is
distinct from most other projects of this scale. The grocery store will offer pre-packaged
foods or snacks, as defined by the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC), and it will not sell
alcohol or tobacco products. In addition, the fueling station will feature four hydrogen fuel
pumps as part of the development making this the first hydrogen fueling station within the
City. The project is beneficial for the City because it will provide goods and services that
are currently lacking along East Avenue R, between State Route 14 and 47th Street East.

Access/Circulation

Street improvements will be constructed along 25th Street East and partially along East
Avenue R to ensure proper access to the site from both roads. The City Engineer and the
Los Angeles County Fire Department have reviewed the project and confirmed that it is
designed to provide safe vehicular access and flow.

Operations

The fueling station and grocery store will operate 24 hours a day and have three
employees for each eight-hour shift. Security cameras will be installed, and access will
be shared with the Palmdale Sheriff's Station. In addition, the drive-through car wash will
operate from sunrise to sunset.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an Initial Study was
prepared to determine whether the project would have a significant effect on the
environment. The Initial Study analyzed the potential for environmental impacts, and all
topics were found to have either no impact, a less than significant impact, or a less than
significant impact with mitigation incorporated. Mitigation measures for biological
resources and cultural resources, geology/soils, noise, and tribal cultural resources were
included to reduce impacts to a less than significant level. As such, an MND and MMRP
were prepared and circulated in accordance with CEQA Guidelines.

10.  Description of Project:

Beyond Food Mart, Inc. (Applicant) is requesting the approval of a General Plan Amendment
(GPA) and Zone Change (ZC), Tentative Parcel Map (TPM), a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) and
Site Plan Review (SPR) to construct and operate a ten-island fueling station, a 7,258-square-foot
grocery store, and a 2,127-square-foot drive-through carwash (see Figure 1 – Site Plan). The
Project Site consists of four parcels totaling approximately 5.6 acres and is located on the
northwest corner of the intersection of 25th Street East and East Avenue R (see Figures 2 and 3
for Regional Location and Site Vicinity). The TPM would subdivide the Project Site into two
parcels. Development of the Proposed Project would occur only on the approximately
110,657-square foot eastern parcel, shown as Parcel 2. Future development of Parcel 1 is not
analyzed in this document and would require a separate application and CEQA analysis.

Access to the Proposed Project will be provided by two 40-foot driveways, one along 25th Street
East and the other along East Avenue R. Uses proposed for the Project Site include a passenger
car gasoline fueling station to be composed of eight fueling islands to include 16 fueling positions
(dispensers) on the southerly portion of the site. The gasoline fueling station includes two
underground storage tanks (USTs). The gasoline fueling islands would be located under a
4,211 square-foot canopy which is proposed at a height of 19 feet, six inches. There will be
another canopy adjacent to the gasoline fueling station for two islands with four hydrogen pumps.
The hydrogen storage tank would be located north of the canopy.

The Proposed Project would include a total of 40 passenger car parking spaces (including two
handicap accessible spaces) for the fueling station, carwash, and grocery store. Two additional
spaces will be provided for electric vehicles (EV). The proposed grocery store and fueling station
are anticipated to operate 24 hours a day and seven days a week. The car wash use shall operate
daily between the hours of 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM. The Proposed Project will include 12 full-time
employees.

The Project Site is within the Mixed Use 2 (MU 2) land use designation and is zoned Mixed Use
2 (MU 2). The Proposed Project requires approval of a General Plan Amendment and Zone
Change to Neighborhood Commercial (NC) to allow for the Proposed Project with subsequent
approval of a CUP and SPR.

1.1  EVALUATION FORMAT

This Initial Study is prepared in compliance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Guidelines. This format of the study is presented as follows. The project is evaluated based upon
its effect on twenty (20) major categories of environmental factors. Each factor is reviewed by
responding to a series of questions regarding the impact of the project on each element of the
overall factor. The Initial Study Checklist provides a formatted analysis that provides a
determination of the effect of the project on the factor and its elements. The effect of the project
is categorized into one of the following four categories of possible determinations:

  Potentially  Less than  Less than  No Impact
  Significant  Significant  Significant
  Impact  with Mitigation

Substantiation is then provided to justify each determination. One of the four following conclusions
is then provided as a summary of the analysis for each of the major environmental factors.

1. Therefore, no impacts are identified or anticipated, and no mitigation measures are required.
2. Therefore, no significant adverse impacts are identified or anticipated, and no mitigation
  measures are required.
3. Possible significant adverse impacts have been identified or anticipated and the following
  mitigation measures are required as a condition of project approval to reduce these impacts to a
  level below significant. The required mitigation measures are: (List mitigation measures)
4. Significant adverse impacts have been identified or anticipated. An Environmental Impact Report
  (EIR) is required to evaluate these impacts, which are: (List the impacts requiring analysis within
  the EIR).

At the end of the analysis the required mitigation measures are restated and categorized as being
either self- monitoring or as requiring a Mitigation Monitoring and Reporting Program.

1.4  EVALUATION OF ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS

  1. A brief explanation is required for all answers except “No Impact” answers that are
  adequately supported by the information sources a lead agency cites. A “No Impact”
  answer is adequately supported if the referenced information sources show that the impact
  simply does not apply to projects like the one involved (e.g., the project falls outside a fault
  rupture zone). A “No Impact” answer should be explained where it is based on project-
  specific factors as well as general standards (e.g., the project will not expose sensitive
  receptors to pollutants, based on a project-specific screening analysis).

  2. All answers must take account of the whole action involved, including offsite as well as
  onsite, cumulative as well as project-level, indirect as well as direct, and construction as
  well as operational impacts.

  3. Once the lead agency has determined that a particular physical impact may occur, then
  the checklist answers must indicate whether the impact is potentially significant, less than
  significant with mitigation, or less than significant. “Potentially Significant Impact” is
  appropriate if substantial evidence exists that an effect may be significant. If one or more
  “Potentially Significant Impact” entries are marked when the determination is made, an
  EIR is required.

  4. “Negative Declaration: Less Than Significant with Mitigation Incorporated” applies where
  the incorporation of mitigation measures has reduced an effect from “Potentially
  Significant Impact” to a “Less Than Significant Impact.” The lead agency must describe
  the mitigation measures and briefly explain how they reduce the effect to a less than
  significant level (mitigation measures from earlier analyses may be cross-referenced).

  5. Earlier analyses may be used where, pursuant to the tiering, program EIR, or other CEQA
  process, an effect has been adequately analyzed in an earlier EIR or negative declaration.
  Section 15063(c)(3)(D). In this case, a brief discussion should identify the following:

  a. Earlier Analysis Used. Identify and state where they are available for review.

  b. Impacts Adequately Addressed. Identify which effects from the above checklist were
  within the scope of and adequately analyzed in an earlier document pursuant to
  applicable legal standards, and state whether such effects were addressed by
  mitigation measures based on the earlier analysis.

  c. Mitigation Measures. For effects that are “Less than Significant with Mitigation
  Measures Incorporated,” describe the mitigation measures which were incorporated
  or refined from the earlier document and the extent to which they address site-specific

  SECTION 2.0 – PROJECT DESCRIPTION

2.1  PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT

The City formally initiated the environmental process for the project with the preparation of this
Initial Study (IS). The IS screens out those impacts that would be less than significant and do not
warrant mitigation, while identifying those issues that require further mitigation to reduce impacts
to a less than significant level. As identified in the following analyses, project impacts related to
various environmental issues either do not occur, are less than significant (when measured
against established significance thresholds) or have been rendered less than significant through
implementation of mitigation measures. Based on these analytical conclusions, this IS supports
adoption of a Mitigated Negative Declaration (MND) for the proposed project. This Initial Study
has been prepared in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and the
State CEQA Guidelines.

CEQA permits the incorporation by reference of all or portions of other documents that are
generally available to the public. The IS has been prepared utilizing information from City planning
and environmental documents, technical studies specifically prepared for the project, and other
publicly available data. The documents utilized in the IS are identified in Section 3.0 and are
hereby incorporated by reference. These documents are available for review at the City of
Palmdale, Economic and Community Development Department.

Pursuant to Section 15367 of the State CEQA Guidelines, the City of Palmdale is the Lead Agency
in the preparation of this Initial Study. The City has primary responsibility for approval or denial of
this project. The intended use of this Initial Study is to provide adequate environmental analysis
related to project construction and operation activities of the Proposed Project.

2.2  PROJECT LOCATION

The Project Site consists of four parcels totaling approximately 5.6 acres and is located east of
State Route 14 and south of Palmdale Boulevard. It is located on the northwest corner of East
Avenue R and 25th Street East. The property is within a primarily residential and commercial area
of the City, and adjacent to Palmdale High School.

2.3  PROJECT DESCRIPTION

Beyond Food Mart, Inc. (Applicant) is requesting the approval of a General Plan Amendment
(GPA) and Zone Change (ZC), Tentative Parcel Map (TPM), Conditional Use Permit (CUP), and
Site Plan Review (SPR) to construct and operate a ten-island fueling station, a 7,258-square-foot
grocery store, and a 2,127-square-foot drive-through carwash (see Figure 1 – Site Plan). The
Project Site consists of four parcels totaling approximately 5.6 acres and is located on the
northwest corner of the intersection of 25th Street East and East Avenue R (see Figures 2 and 3
for Regional Location and Site Vicinity). The TPM would subdivide the Project Site into two
parcels. Development of the Proposed Project would occur only on the approximately
110,657-square foot eastern parcel, shown as Parcel 2. Future development of Parcel 1 is not
analyzed in this document and would require a separate application and CEQA analysis.

Access to the Proposed Project will be provided by two 40-foot driveways, one along 25th Street
East and the other along East Avenue R. Uses proposed for the Project Site include a passenger
car gasoline fueling station to be composed of eight fueling islands to include 16 fueling positions

  Desert Tortoise
  The desert tortoise is a State and federally listed threatened species. In 1992, the US Bureau
  of Land Management issued the California Statewide Desert Tortoise Management Policy
  which included categorizing habitat into three levels of classification. In April 1993, the BLM
  amended the California Desert Conservation Area (CDCA) plan to delineate these three
  categories of desert tortoise habitat on public lands. Although habitat categories apply only to
  public lands administered by the BLM, regulatory agencies typically determine habitat
  compensation ratios based on the nearest BLM habitat categories. With the adoption of the
  West Mojave Plan, all lands that are outside Desert Wildlife Management Areas, including the
  Project Site, are characterized as Category 3 Habitat, which is the lowest priority management
  area for viable populations of the desert tortoise.

  No suitable habitat for desert tortoise exists within the Project Site or surrounding area. There
  are no documented desert tortoise occurrences within the Project Site or the surrounding area
  and this species is not expected to occur within the Project Site. Due to the high level of on-
  site human disturbance and the isolation of the site by surrounding development, the Project
  Site and immediate vicinity is no longer considered suitable habitat for the desert tortoise.

  Mohave Ground Squirrel
  The Mohave ground squirrel (MGS) is a State listed threatened species. In the western Mohave
  Desert, the geographic range of the species is considered to lie west of the Mojave River.
  However, in the Victorville and Barstow areas, there are records of Mohave ground squirrel
  occurrence on the east side of the Mohave River. MGS is listed as threatened by CDFW due
  to habitat loss, fragmentation, and deterioration. The Project Site falls within the historic range
  of the MGS but is located outside and to the south of the MGS Conservation Area set forth in
  the West Mojave Plan.

  Jennings conducted an MGS habitat assessment of the Project Site. The habitat assessment
  for MGS included a pedestrian field assessment, a review of reported occurrences of the MGS
  in the region and adherence to CDFW's criteria for assessing potential impacts to the MGS.
  Adequate cover and forage for MGS appeared to be limited within and around the Project Site.
  No winterfat (Eurotia lanata), nor spiny hopsage (Grayia spinosa) were found on the Project
  Site, which are considered important forage for MGS. No streams or washes were noted on
  the Project Site. Absence of this habitat feature further lessens the likelihood of MGS presence
  on the Project Site or their ability to persist during long term drought conditions. No wildlife
  corridors are expected to exist between the closest core MGS population and the Project Site.

  The Project Site is also surrounded by existing development. The scattered development within
  the project vicinity further isolates the site from MGS, as these land uses prevent movement
  from the known populations to the north. Because the Project Site has low quality habitat for
  MGS, is within the historical range but not within or near any current or recent occurrences, is
  surrounded by development, and the Project Site is subject to ongoing human disturbances
  such as foot traffic and vehicle traffic, this species is considered absent from the Project Site
  and presence/absence surveys for this species are not warranted or recommended.

  Burrowing Owl
  The burrowing owl (BUOW) is a state and federal SSC. The BUOW is a migratory bird
  protected by the international treaty under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 and by State
  law under the California Fish and Game Code. The conditions present onsite appeared to be
  suitable for BUOW. As such a BUOW survey was completed. The assessment survey was
  structured, in part, to detect BUOW. The result of the survey was that no evidence of BUOW
  was found in the survey area. No burrows of appropriate size, aspect, or shape were located
  and no BUOW pellets, feathers, or whitewash were found. No burrowing owl individuals were
  observed. Additionally, the Project Site was found to contain no suitable habitat for this species
  as the soils were not friable and no suitable burrow surrogate species was observed.
  Therefore, no further studies or surveys are recommended.

  The Fish and Game Commission provided notice that the western Joshua tree is a candidate
  species as defined by Section 2068 of the Fish and Game Code. There are currently no western
  Joshua trees present on-site. Therefore, there are no potential impacts to this species.

a) Would the project result in generation of a substantial temporary or permanent increase in

  Less than Significant with Mitigation Incorporated. A Noise Impact Analysis, dated
  September 26, 2022 and revised December 21, 2023, was prepared for the Proposed Project
  by Ganddini Group, Inc. (see Appendix J for report). The unit of measurement used to describe
  a noise level is the decibel (dB). The human ear is not equally sensitive to all frequencies within
  the sound spectrum. Therefore, the “A-weighted” noise scale, which weights the frequencies
  to which humans are sensitive, is used for measurements. Noise levels using A-weighted
  measurements are written dB(A) or dBA. Noise standards for land use compatibility are stated
  in terms of the Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL) and the Day-Night Average Noise
  Level (DNL). CNEL is a 24-hour weighted average measure of community noise. CNEL is
  obtained by adding five decibels to sound levels in the evening (7:00 PM to 10:00PM), and by
  adding ten decibels to sound levels at night (10:00 PM to 7:00 AM). This weighting accounts
  for the increased human sensitivity to noise during the evening and nighttime hours. DNL is a
  very similar 24-hour average measure that weights only the nighttime hours. The equivalent
  continuous noise level, Leq, is a level of steady state sound that in a stated time period, and a
  stated location, has the same A-weighted sound energy as the time-varying sound.

  Less than Significant with Mitigation Incorporated. California Assembly Bill 52 (AB52) was
  approved by Governor Brown on September 25, 2014. AB52 specifies that CEQA projects with
  an effect that may cause a substantial adverse change in the significance of a tribal cultural
  resource may have a significant effect on the environment. As such, the bill requires lead
  agency consultation with California Native American tribes traditionally and culturally affiliated
  with the geographic area of a Proposed Project, if the tribe requested to the lead agency, in
  writing, to be informed of proposed projects in that geographic area. The legislation further
  requires that the tribe-requested consultation be completed prior to determining whether a
  negative declaration, mitigated negative declaration, or environmental impact report is required
  for a project.

  As required by CEQA, AB 52 consultation is performed between the lead government agency
  and California Native American tribes who have requested notification of projects in their
  traditional area.

  Senate Bill 18 (SB 18) requires cities and counties to conduct consultations with California
  Native American tribes before the local officials adopt or amend their general plans. These
  consultations are for preserving or mitigating impacts to Native American historic, cultural,
  sacred sites, features, and objects located within the city or county.

  Less than Significant Impact. Cumulative impacts are defined as two or more individual
  effects that, when considered together, are considerable or that compound or increase other
  environmental impacts. The cumulative impact from several projects is the change in the
  environment that results from the incremental impact of the development when added to the
  impacts of other closely related past, present, and reasonably foreseeable or probable future
  developments. Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor, but collectively
  significant, developments taking place over a period. The CEQA Guidelines, Section 15130 (a)
  and (b), states:

  (a) Cumulative impacts shall be discussed when the project’s incremental effect is
  cumulatively considerable.

  (b) The discussion of cumulative impacts shall reflect the severity of the impacts and their
  likelihood of occurrence, but the discussion need not provide as great detail as is provided
  of the effects attributable to the project. The discussion should be guided by the standards
  of practicality and reasonableness.
